questions.q: What is change control, as defined in this lesson?
options: A single person's final sign-off on a deployment
A tool used only to roll back failed deployments
A Salesforce feature that automatically blocks all declarative changes
The formal process of requesting, assessing, approving, scheduling, implementing, and verifying a change before and after it reaches production
questions.explain: Change control is the full lifecycle -- request, assess, approve, schedule, implement, verify -- not just a single approval step.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say declarative changes create a genuine challenge for change-control policy on Salesforce?
options: Declarative changes are always low-risk by definition, so they need no policy at all

Declarative changes can be just as consequential as code changes (a bad validation rule or Flow can block sales or corrupt data), but they don't automatically go through the same build-test-deploy pipeline code does
Salesforce doesn't allow declarative changes to reach production
Declarative changes can only be made by developers, never by admins
questions.explain: Declarative changes can be made quickly, directly in production-affecting configuration, and can be just as risky as code -- but a policy focused only on code deployments can accidentally leave them ungoverned.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a standard change?
options: A change made during an active production incident
Any change made through Apex code, regardless of risk
A low-risk, well-understood, repeatable change that follows a pre-approved template without needing individual case-by-case approval
A change that always requires executive sign-off
questions.explain: Standard changes are pre-approved, repeatable, and low-risk -- like adding a new picklist value using an established convention -- so they skip the full individual approval cycle.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say emergency changes still require a full after-the-fact review?
options: So that the faster emergency-approval path doesn't quietly become a way to skip governance any time a change feels urgent
Because emergency changes are illegal and must be reversed immediately
Because emergency changes are never actually approved by anyone
Because after-the-fact review replaces the need for any approval at all during the emergency
questions.explain: Emergency changes get a faster approval path to address active incidents, but the mandatory after-the-fact review exists specifically to prevent 'urgent' from becoming an excuse to bypass governance routinely.

questions.q: In the risk-based gating approach to declarative vs. programmatic changes described in this lesson, what determines how much scrutiny a change gets?
options: Whether the change was declarative or programmatic, with declarative changes always getting less scrutiny no matter what
The actual impact of the change -- how many users are affected, whether it touches a regulated process, whether it's reversible -- regardless of whether it happens to be declarative or code
Whichever team made the change gets to decide its own scrutiny level
Only changes made on a Friday require any review at all
questions.explain: Risk-based gating classifies changes by actual impact rather than by mechanism, so a high-risk declarative change gets the same full review a high-risk code change would, and a low-risk version of either gets a lighter path.
